newsitem.title: USA: White House worried about partisan hearings.
newsitem.headline: White House worried about partisan hearings.

text.p: The White House expressed concern Wednesday that Republicans will use congressional hearings on political campaign fund raising to score partisan points against Democrats.

White House officials were trying to make a pre-emptive appeal for fairness as Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson prepared to open hearings Tuesday in his Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on fund raising for last year's campaigns.
"Up to now, there has not been evidence of an even-handed inquiry," said White House special counsel Lanny Davis.
As an example he cited the number of subpoenas the committee has directed toward Democratic targets -- 442 -- compared to only 34 against Republican targets.
Of equal concern was the prospect of partisan hearings in the House conducted by Indiana Republican Representative Dan Burton's House Government Reform and Oversight Committee.

A top lawyer in that committee, John Rowley, a former U.S. attorney, abruptly resigned Tuesday after repeated clashes with the committee's top investigator. White House officials feared the committee was losing an even-handed authority.

"It's a concern when a former U.S. attorney who has been charged with fairly conducting this inquiry says he's not allowed to operate in a professional manner. In a way, that's flabbergasting," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

The hearings were to review whether any laws were broken in the way money was raised for last year's campaigns. They were called after disclosures over the past nine months about questionable fund-raising practices and questions as whether Chinese interests sought to direct donations to President Clinton's re-election campaign.
One White House official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, described the hearing process to date as "sheer partisan politics" and "one-sided."

Officials urged Thompson to pursue the end result of campaign finance reform, a frequent appeal made by Clinton even as he continues raising millions of dollars through the type of large, unregulated "soft money" contributions that he has said should be banned.

"It's apparent that the Republican Party right now, having benefited from the system, isn't interested in reforming," Davis said. "Only if both parties are scrutinised can there be a basis for campaign finance reform."

Party lawyers said the Democratic National Committee has sent about 120 boxes of documents containing about 275,000 pages to each of the Senate and House committees conducting the investigation. They complained the information requested by the committees was too broad in scope.

But Paul Clark, spokesman for the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, said the broad scope has been necessary because even the DNC has judged nearly $3 million in contributions to have been illegal or improper or questionable at best and returned it to the donors.
"In order to find out what happened in the 1996 cycle ... we need to subpoena documents and testimony," he said.

As Democrats groused, the Republican National Committee said Wednesday it had produced more than 80,000 pages of documents in response to inquiries from the Senate and House committees after an exhaustive two-month search of office and warehouse space equal in size two football fields.
"We believe in openness and full disclosure and we practice what we preach," said RNC Chairman Jim Nicholson. "The fact is, we have been open and the Democrats have not."

Nicholson stressed that he had no reason to believe Republicans had broken any law, but charged that Democrats had knowingly violated campaign financing regulations and "orchestrated a cover-up directly from the White House."
